deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Unregulated Relocation

For dental practitioners, a relocation clause is not merely a logistical inconvenience; it is a potential practice-ending event. While landlords retain the right to reconfigure a building for redevelopment or to accommodate larger tenants, an unmitigated relocation clause allows them to move your practice into a 'dead zone' within the center. In the context of a dental office, the technical requirements for plumbing, specialized electrical loads for imaging equipment, and lead-lined walls for X-ray shielding are non-negotiable. A landlord-driven move to a space lacking these structural capabilities can result in millions of dollars in unbudgeted capital expenditures and significant operational downtime.

The primary 'gotcha' in these clauses is the lack of specificity regarding the 'comparable' nature of the new space. Without strict definitions, a landlord may argue that any space of equal square footage constitutes a valid relocation, ignoring critical factors such as storefront visibility, signage rights, and proximity to high-traffic corridors that drive patient acquisition.

Establishing Market-Standard Protections

To protect your practice's clinical integrity and long-term revenue, your lease must include specific safeguards that go beyond simple rent abatement. A sophisticated dental lease should demand the following protections:

  • Full Reimbursement of Tenant Improvements: The landlord must be contractually obligated to pay for all costs associated with the build-out of the new space, including specialized plumbing, electrical, and medical-grade finishes.
  • Standard of Comparability: The new space must be 'substantially similar' in terms of visibility, foot traffic, and accessibility to your existing patient base.
  • Termination Rights: If the landlord cannot provide a space that meets your pre-defined clinical and regulatory specifications, the tenant must have the right to terminate the lease without penalty.
  • Loss of Goodwill Compensation: Provisions should address the potential loss of revenue resulting from the disruption of established patient patterns and the physical move.

Navigating these technicalities requires more than just a cursory reading of the lease document. Do not let a landlord-friendly relocation clause compromise your practice's future.
